summary: We developed Meteopark, an interactive webpage to demonstrate the results of our experiments using Giovanni and AppEEARS data. We study the effect of humidity on vegetation in five chosen places on Earth. We conclude that, in these areas, precipitation shows a positive correlation with NDVI delayed by one month, meaning that vegetation grows significantly approximately one month after rainfall. This is important because it helps us understand and predict vegetation responses to climate conditions, which can be useful for agriculture, drought monitoring, and environmental protection.
details:
GitHub link: https://github.com/ElParque-NASA-USAL/MeteoPark

What it does / How it works: MeteoPark investigates how rainfall drives vegetation growth across five global regions (2000–2025). It calculates lagged Pearson correlations on climatological anomalies to visualize the exact delay between precipitation and greening, displayed on an interactive dashboard.

Benefits: It eliminates the technical friction of processing heavy geospatial datasets (NetCDF), providing users with sub-second, interactive insights into climate anomalies without writing any code.

Intended impact: Empowers students, researchers, and the public to act as "data detectives," making it effortless to investigate droughts, desertification, and ecological resilience worldwide.

Tools used: NASA AppEEARS, Giovanni, and GIBS/Worldview. Backend: Python (FastAPI, pandas, xarray). Frontend: React + TypeScript (Vite).

How is your project creative? It bridges abstract statistics and physical reality by directly pairing interactive anomaly charts with authentic, dated NASA satellite imagery (true-color and NDVI composites) for the exact region and month analyzed.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Performance: We aggregated massive 3D pixel cubes into lightweight (<50KB) "wide-format" CSVs to ensure instantaneous frontend loading.
  • Statistical Rigor: We analyzed seasonal anomalies (subtracting historical monthly means) to prevent false causation driven by predictable annual cycles.
  • Statistical Roadmap: While our current MVP establishes baseline trend sensitivity using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) linear fits and climatological anomalies, we recognize that climate data often violates normality assumptions. Therefore, we designed our methodological roadmap to transition toward advanced non-parametric inference (STL decomposition, Mann-Kendall tests, Theil-Sen estimators) for outlier-immune trend detection in future iterations.
